# Research brief: java.security.KeyStore and the KeyStoreSpec finding

**Scope and limits.** I used web search only, and I could not open the raw KeyStore.crysl file. Question 4 is therefore not answered from the source itself (see Q4). Search results returned excerpts, not whole pages. I did not inspect repository code or assess exploitability.

## Q1. What KeyStore governs, and what the finding refers to

- **What the class is.** The Javadoc describes `java.security.KeyStore` as <https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html> "a storage facility for cryptographic keys and certificates." It is also summarized at <https://javadoc.scijava.org/Java21/java.base/java/security/package-summary.html>.
- **Three ways to get an instance** (<https://developer.android.com/reference/java/security/KeyStore> and the Java 21 Javadoc):
  - Pass an existing keystore file. The system probes the file's type and returns an implementation with its entries already loaded.
  - Rely on the default type.
  - Name a specific type.
- **Load requirement.** The Javadoc says a keystore must be loaded before it can be accessed, "unless it was already loaded during instantiation" (<https://docs.oracle.com/javase/9/docs/api/java/security/KeyStore.html>). Calls such as `getKey`, `getEntry`, `setEntry` and `store` document a `KeyStoreException` "if the keystore has not been initialized (loaded)" (<https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/KeyStore.html>).
- **Reloading.** The Android reference notes that calling `load` on an already-loaded keystore reinitializes and reloads it (<https://developer.android.com/reference/java/security/KeyStore>).
- **What an InvalidSequenceOfMethodCalls finding refers to.** It is not a documented Java API event or value. It is a CrySL-style finding about an object's call sequence. CrySL describes the ORDER section as a regular-expression-like description of the events expected on each object (<https://eclipse.dev/cognicrypt/documentation/crysl/>). The EVENTS section lists the methods of the "class under specification" (<https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04950v1>). The compiler turns ORDER into a state machine. A finding means the observed calls on a tracked object do not follow that machine.
- **What the finding does not mean.** The Javadoc defines no "valid sequence" beyond the load-before-access requirement. The finding is a property of the rule's model, not of the Java API contract.
- **Per the supplied input, not independently confirmed.** The rule's protocol is `Get, Load, ((GetEntry?, GetKey) | (SetEntry, Store))*`.

## Q2. Documented correct and safe usage, and remediation

- **Sequence.** The Javadoc examples show `getInstance`, then `load(InputStream, char[])`, then entry access. They show `setEntry` for writes and `store(OutputStream, char[])` to persist (<https://docs.oracle.com/javase/6/docs/api/java/security/KeyStore.html>). Passing `null` as the stream to `load` creates an empty keystore (<https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/KeyStore.html>).
- **Passwords.** The Javadoc documents the `load` password as one used "to check the integrity" or to unlock the keystore, and it may be `null`. If no password is given for integrity checking, integrity checking is not performed (<https://developer.android.com/reference/java/security/KeyStore>). The examples take the password as `char[]` from `getPassword()`.
- **`getInstance(File, …)`.** The `getInstance(File, char[])` and `getInstance(File, LoadStoreParameter)` overloads return an already-loaded keystore. The Android reference says no separate `load` call is needed there (<https://developer.android.com/reference/java/security/KeyStore>; Microsoft's binding text at <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/java.security.keystore?view=net-android-35.0> says the same). The overloads are listed at <https://cr.openjdk.org/~pminborg/panama/21/v1/javadoc/java.base/java/security/class-use/KeyStore.html>.
- **Writing entries.** `setKeyEntry` and `setCertificateEntry` are separate documented APIs. `setKeyEntry` is documented at <https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html>.
- **Android.**
  - The documented pattern is `KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore")`, then `load(null)`, then `getEntry(alias, null)` (<https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/keystore>).
  - `SecretKeyEntry.getSecretKey()` is shown in <https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/risks/hardcoded-cryptographic-secrets>.
  - `KeyProtection` shows `setEntry` followed by `getKey("key1", null)`. It also says to obtain keys with `getKey(String, null)` or `getEntry(String, null)` (<https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/keystore/KeyProtection>).
  - None of these Android examples call `store`. I did not find any official text on `AndroidKeyStoreSpi.engineStore`, so the input's claim about `UnsupportedOperationException` is unverified here.
- **Remediation text.** I found no official source that gives a remediation for "incorrect call order" as such. The Javadoc only documents the exceptions above. Choosing a fix is out of scope.

## Q3. Compatibility

- **Default type.**
  - The Java 8 Javadoc says `getDefaultType()` returns the `keystore.type` property value, or "jks" if it is unset (<https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/KeyStore.html>).
  - The Java 22 and 27 Javadocs say "pkcs12" instead (<https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/22/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html>, <https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html>).
  - Applications that do not want a hard-coded type are directed to `getDefaultType()`.
- **JEP 229** (<https://openjdk.org/jeps/229>):
  - New keystores default to PKCS12.
  - Existing keystores do not change.
  - Applications may still name a type explicitly.
  - Applications must keep working across JDK releases, so JKS and PKCS12 keystores must stay accessible.
- **Required type.** The Java 21 Javadoc states that every Java platform implementation must support PKCS12 (<https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html>).
- **Standard types.** The standard types listed include jceks, jks, dks and pkcs11 (<https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html>). The JDK 8 guide also lists them (<https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/StandardNames.html>).
- **Format limits.** The JDK 8 Javadoc states that a jks keystore needs a protected key encoded as `EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo` (PKCS #8) (<https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/KeyStore.html>).
- **Android.**
  - The reference table lists AndroidKeyStore as API 18+ (<https://developer.android.com/reference/java/security/KeyStore>).
  - The keystore guide says the provider was introduced in Android 4.3 (API 18) (<https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/keystore>).
- **Dual-format behavior.**
  - I found only unofficial sources for `keystore.type.compat` and dual JKS/PKCS12 loading: <https://nhimg.org/java-keystores-jks-pkcs12-guide> and <https://github.com/robolectric/robolectric/issues/5496>.
  - I did not find the official Security Developer's Guide page, so that is unresolved.
- **Open edge case.** The JDK bug report <https://bugs.openjdk.org/browse/JDK-8231107> states that passing `null` as the password to `store` on PKCS12 results in an empty `char[]` being used. This is a bug-tracker description, not specification text.
- **Wire formats and migration.** Persisted formats are the keystore file types above. The sources describe no wire format. The only documented migration path is JEP 229's default-type change.

## Q4. What KeyStore.crysl matches

**I could not retrieve <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyStore.crysl>.** I cannot quote the matching clause verbatim and cannot confirm the rule's text.
